analysis.headline: The 3-year fps delay roughly doubles the odds that Embraer becomes an independent third single-aisle player, from about 6% (range 2-13%) with fps in 2041 to about 11% (range 4-24%) with fps in 2044. It is still a long shot. The delay opens a real gap. The board's unserved demand rises from 1,920 to 5,040 aircraft, and an entrant timed to Embraer's realistic schedule moves from clearly negative to about break-even (judgement). The binding constraint is still money: a 150-210 seat clean sheet would cost $15-25B, against a market cap of about $13B. Two other things hold the odds down. Embraer has a habit of waiting for Boeing to move first. And the delay makes a Boeing–Embraer Joint Venture more attractive. That Joint Venture is about as likely as independent entry (about 10% rising to 12%), and it would not create a third player.

The CSeries grew from $2.1B (2005) to $5.4B at certification (Dec 2015). The board's fps 10-year bill is $55.25B and NGSA's is $30.07B. The war game uses $30B of fps development capex.

capability_facts.fact: My sizing (calculation from the rows above). A $15B programme is 1.1x market cap, 2.0x 2025 revenue, 17x 2025 adjusted EBITDA, 5.4x consensus 2026-30 free cash flow and 8.8x the E2. Spread over 8 years it is about 4.9x the 2025 investment level. At $10B and $25B the ratio to market cap is 0.8x and 1.9x. Judgement: Embraer can fund about $4-5B itself by 2035 (consensus net cash of $2.2B in 2030 plus about five years of roughly $0.6B free cash flow). Partners would therefore have to fund about 65-80% of a $15-25B programme.
capability_facts.source: Computed from the rows above; the self-funding estimate is my judgement

capability_facts.fact: Under the board's own leverage-penalty rule (alpha 0.30), a $15B programme entering service in 2042 costs Embraer $2.31B of present value if Embraer debt-funds it alone. The penalty falls to $0.15B if partners fund 70%.

The capex Boeing could pay and still break even: $43.2B (2041) and $32.1B (2044).

current_status_facts.fact: As of Oct 2026 Embraer has not launched or committed to a single-aisle to rival the A320neo and 737 MAX.
current_status_facts.source: Leeham, 4 Sep 2026: https://leehamnews.com/2026/09/04/will-embraer-go-big-by-developing-a-large-narrowbody-jet/ (paywalled; headline and summary only)

current_status_facts.fact: On 8 May 2026 the CEO said Embraer is 'making studies for a new cycle of products... either a commercial jet or a business jet... we talk to all of them' (asked about Rolls-Royce). He added that it is investing in 'aerostructures, wings, cockpits... to be ready to develop a new airplane'.
current_status_facts.source: Transcripts PDF p13 and p15 (FQ1 2026 call)

current_status_facts.fact: On 4 Nov 2025 the CEO said new products 'could refer to Commercial Aviation, meaning larger planes than E195-E2. It could be larger or smaller', and that 'we don't have a time line definition'. In Nov 2025 he told Forbes Brasil there is 'no deadline'.

On 27 Feb 2025 the CEO said the plan to 2030 is 'to make sure we will have a very healthy cash generation to support a potential next move', with revenue 'beyond $10 billion' by the end of the decade excluding Eve. On 7 May 2024 he said there were no plans 'to develop or launch a narrowbody... in the next few years'.
current_status_facts.source: Transcripts PDF p128 (FQ4 2024 call) and p230 (FQ1 2024 call)

current_status_facts.fact: Embraer's own stated decision rule, 31 Oct 2016: 'I don't think that we'll launch any new aircraft that will be larger than the E2, if Boeing and Airbus are still in this segment... if they decide to move upwards... and give up a little bit of this market... we will look again.' In Mar 2011 Embraer waited for Boeing's choice before deciding whether to go larger, then chose the E2.
current_status_facts.source: Transcripts PDF p694-695 (FQ3 2016 call) and p1089 (FQ4 2010 call, 25 Mar 2011)

current_status_facts.fact: Leeham reported on 12 Jan 2026 that Embraer is exploring a 180-240 seat design but is unlikely to confirm it in 2026. On 12 Jun 2026 Embraer's R&T director said 'We do have a single aisle aircraft as one of our potential products for the future.'

Partner search. In May 2024 the WSJ reported that Embraer had sounded out Saudi Arabia's PIF and manufacturers in Turkey, India and South Korea. The Air Current reports talks with Japan. In Jul 2026 Seoul said it is weighing a development-stage role in 'Embraer's planned next-generation airliner' but that talks are at 'a very early stage' with no terms set. KAI and Embraer signed a structures MoU on 28 Jul 2026, Turkish Aerospace signed an E2-production MoU on 1 Apr 2025, and Mubadala signed a framework in Jul 2026. No sovereign equity commitment has been confirmed.

Brazil's state backing is export credit and small R&D money, not launch aid. BNDES lent about R$28.8B to Embraer in 2023-25, mostly for exports. In Apr 2026 it approved R$279M for innovation. There is no development loan for a new programme.

Airbus CEO Faury said in late Jun 2026 that Embraer should 'think twice' about entering the market against Airbus, Boeing 'and now COMAC'. Airbus targets an NGSA launch around 2030, with entry into service in the second half of the 2030s.

Boeing–Embraer history. Boeing terminated the $4.2B deal for 80% of Embraer's commercial arm on 25 Apr 2020, and Embraer called the termination wrongful. The arbitration ended on 16 Sep 2024 with Boeing paying $150M under a collar agreement, against roughly $300M of costs Embraer had estimated. Boeing had first sought Embraer about 3 months after Airbus took the CSeries, for its engineering talent and capacity, and called the deal 'not a must do'.
current_status_facts.source: Transcripts PDF p483 (27 Apr 2020) and p188/p190 (FQ3 2024 call); Embraer 20-F FY2024: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1355444/000119312525069283/d914513d20f.htm; https://www.tipranks.com/news/the-fly/embraer-award-from-boeing-disappointing-but-reaction-overdone-says-bofa; evidence B-1326, B-1420, B-1567, B-1382, B-1674, B-2131 (boeing/evidence.jsonl)

current_status_facts.fact: E2 momentum. Embraer sold 'almost 200 E2s' in 2025 and has 24 E2 operators. In Q2 2026 its backlog reached a record $34.5B. In Mar 2026 Finnair ordered E2s (134 seats) and said neither incumbent has MAX or neo slots until 2032-2033.
current_status_facts.source: Transcripts PDF p15 (8 May 2026) and p31 (Finnair call, 23 Mar 2026); Q2 2026 coverage (Leeham URL above)

current_status_facts.fact: Competition for the same overflow. Boeing's 737 line is cleared to 47 a month (May-Jun 2026) and targets 52 a month in early 2027. COMAC delivered about 15 C919s in 2025, has no EASA certification, and targets 150 a year by 2028 and 200 by 2029.

entry_paths.path: Independent (counts as a third player): an Embraer-led clean-sheet 180-210 seat family, funded with sovereign or industrial partners (PIF, Korea, Japan, Turkey, India) and powered by a new-generation engine.
entry_paths.why_delay_changes_it: Fact: the delay grows the board's unserved demand at an Airbus capacity of 1,200 a year from 1,920 to 5,040 aircraft over 2037-56. In 2045 the gap is 360 a year instead of 140, and it is still 160 a year in 2055 instead of zero (vacuum.json; wf/entrant2.json). For an entrant on Embraer's realistic timing (entry into service 2042, $15B), board-convention NPV improves from -2.44 to -0.49, or from -1.51 to +0.43 if it also wins a 5% slice of the whole market. Both board equilibria at 2044 have Boeing on Do Nothing for the narrowbody, and the war game also said no-go. Judgement: this is the nearest the market gets to Embraer's own 2016 trigger ('give up a little bit of this market'). Against that, Boeing's fps decision moves to about 2037, after the 2035 cutoff, so Embraer would have to move first, which it has never done against Boeing.
binding_constraints: Financing: $15-25B all-in against a market cap of about $13.2B. Embraer can fund about $4-5B itself by 2035 (judgement), so partners must cover 65-80%, and none has committed.
Embraer's habit of waiting for Boeing (2011) and its 2016 rule, plus management's 'no deadline' financial discipline.
Accessible demand is smaller than the board shows: the 737 line at 47-52 a month and COMAC take part of the overflow, and Airbus can add capacity.
Incumbent response: Faury's 'think twice' warning, and the CSeries precedent, which ended in a trade case and Bombardier's exit.
Engineering bandwidth may go first to a large business jet: Executive Aviation earned R$1.47B in 2025 against R$336M for Commercial.
Volume: the E2 reached 44 a year 7 years after first delivery, so 100 a year by 2045 needs a launch by about 2032.

entry_paths.path: Independent, smaller step (counts only if 150+ seats): a new roughly 150-170 seat aircraft above the E195-E2. It is cheaper, roughly $8-12B (judgement).
entry_paths.why_delay_changes_it: Judgement: it gains less from the delay. The board's vacuum sits in Airbus's core 170-200+ seat volume, while a 150-170 seater meets the A220-300 and A320neo and competes with Embraer's own E195-E2. Its lower cost means it relies less on sovereign money, so the delay helps only a little.
binding_constraints: Cannibalises the E195-E2, which tops out at 132-136 seats typically and 146 at most, against rivals' 170-180.
Airbus can answer cheaply at the bottom of the band (judgement).
Still needs a new engine at about 25-30k lbf of thrust (judgement); P&W is the natural fit.

entry_paths.path: Boeing's partner (does NOT count as a third player): the board's 'fps via Embraer' Joint Venture, or Boeing buying back Embraer's commercial arm. Embraer's engineering goes into Boeing's product, and the independent entrant disappears.
entry_paths.why_delay_changes_it: Fact: on war-game Joint Venture terms the board gives +2.21 (2041) and -0.83 (2044) against Do Nothing, versus Solo at +1.06 and -2.53. In the delayed war game the Joint Venture was Boeing's best fps form (-0.73). So the delay makes the Joint Venture the preferred form if Boeing launches at all. It also makes a launch less likely: no pure equilibrium includes fps from 2043, and the war game said no-go. Judgement: P(launch) of about 0.7 times P(Joint Venture given launch) of about 0.15 at 2041 gives about 10%. About 0.35 times 0.35 at 2044 gives about 12%. The board's $100B price (-17.05 / -15.95) is not credible. It is 1.8x the Solo bill and about 7.6x Embraer's market cap; Boeing could buy all of Embraer and still fund Solo for less.
binding_constraints: Embraer cannot pay 35% of $55.25B ($19.3B, 1.5x its market cap) without its own sovereign co-investors. A war-game Go needs it to pay more than 47.9%.
Trust after the 2020 termination and the arbitration settled in 2024; Brazil's government stance (judgement).
Boeing's own launch economics at 2044: the break-even capex Boeing could pay is $32.1B on Joint Venture terms, against a $35.9B share.

entry_paths.path: No entry (baseline): Embraer stays below 150 seats with the E2 and spends its next cycle on a larger business jet or defence.
entry_paths.why_delay_changes_it: Judgement: this is the residual. The delay pulls about 7 points out of this baseline, about 5 into independent entry and about 2 into the Joint Venture.
binding_constraints: Embraer's profit is in Executive Aviation, Services and Defence, not Commercial Aviation (Segments.xls 2025).
Management is weighing buybacks and pays out 25% of net income (transcripts p64 and p5), which signals no big programme yet.
Engine and technology maturity: Embraer has shelved a turboprop before for lack of engine gains.

overall.definition: A third player is a company other than Boeing or Airbus that either (a) delivers a 150-210 seat single-aisle by 2045 at 100 or more a year (5% or more of the board's 2,000 a year) to customers outside its home country, or (b) has committed funding to such a programme by 2035. Embraer counts only as an independent competitor, including one with sovereign or industrial co-investors. Entering as Boeing's partner through the board's 'fps via Embraer' Joint Venture does not count. A clean sheet takes 8-10 years to reach service, and the E2 needed 7 years after first delivery to reach 44 a year. Leg (a) therefore cannot be met without a launch by about 2032-33, so P(third player) is essentially P(independent launch by 2035).
overall.method:
The method is a four-stage chain for an independent launch by 2035. All stage probabilities are my judgement, anchored on the facts cited. The ranges come from multiplying the stage ranges, so they are deliberately wide.

The chain is Opportunity x Financing x Engine supply x Commitment by 2035 without being pre-empted.
- fps in 2041: 0.30 x 0.35 x 0.85 x 0.65 = 5.8%, about 6% (range 0.20-0.40 x 0.25-0.50 x 0.80-0.90 x 0.50-0.75 = 2-13%).
- fps in 2044: 0.55 x 0.40 x 0.90 x 0.55 = 10.9%, about 11% (range 0.40-0.70 x 0.30-0.55 x 0.85-0.95 x 0.40-0.65 = 4-24%).

1) Opportunity: 0.30 → 0.55.
- Board facts: unserved demand rises from 1,920 aircraft (peak 240 a year) to 5,040 (peak 400 a year) at an Airbus capacity of 1,200 a year; with Boeing on Do Nothing it is 6,860 (vacuum.json). The brief's entrant (entry into service 2038, $15B) goes from -2.78 to -0.51, and with $20B and a 10% slice from -1.35 to +0.92.
- My runs on Embraer's realistic timing (wf/entrant2.json): entry into service 2042 at $15B gives -2.44 → -0.49, and with a 5% slice -1.51 → +0.43. Entry into service 2043 gives -2.35 → -0.63, and -1.53 → +0.18.
- The board credits Airbus with NGSA margin on aircraft above its 1,200 a year capacity worth $7.95B PV with fps in 2041 and $16.82B with fps in 2044 ($2.15B and $8.81B at 1,320 a year; wf/airbus_overflow.json). That is the prize an entrant would contest.
- The delay leaves Boeing on Do Nothing in both 2044 equilibria, with share pinned at 20% from 2043. That is close to Embraer's 2016 trigger.

Where I disagree with the board's vacuum and entrant numbers (judgement unless cited):
(i) The vacuum comes from the share rule, not from a lack of aircraft. Boeing's existing 737 line, at 47 a month (about 564 a year) and aiming for 52 (about 624), can already build 164-224 a year more than the board's 20% Boeing share of 400 a year. That covers about 40-55% of the 400 a year peak gap with an available product.
(ii) COMAC is chasing China's slice of the gap (targets of 150-200 a year by 2028-29, though it delivered about 15 in 2025).
(iii) The vacuum depends heavily on Airbus capacity. At 1,320 a year the fps-2044 vacuum nearly halves to 2,700 (vacuum.json), and Airbus has every reason to build into it.
(iv) The entrant model is too generous. It assumes a flat 12% margin, no learning-curve losses and no price response from the incumbents, and its 3-year ramp reaches 100 a year in year 1-2, against the E2's 44 a year after 7 years. It also ignores Embraer's balance sheet: the board's own leverage penalty adds $2.31B if Embraer self-funds.
(v) Where the board understates: sovereign partners may accept returns below the cost of capital for industrial-policy reasons. That is why the odds are not near zero.

2) Financing: 0.35 → 0.40. A $15-25B all-in programme is 1.1-1.9x Embraer's roughly $13.2B market cap, against an estimated $4-5B of self-funding capacity by 2035. Talks exist (PIF, Korea, Japan, Turkey, India) but nothing is committed, and BNDES offers export credit, not launch aid. A visibly weaker Boeing makes the sovereign pitch a little stronger.

3) Engine supply: 0.85 → 0.90. Engines are not the binding constraint. P&W is sole source on the E2, is locked out of fps in our war game and cancelled GTF2 in the delayed game, so it has the most to gain. Rolls-Royce wants a route back into narrowbodies. CFM has a placeholder Embraer lever that is PV-negative. The engine board is unchanged by the delay (narrowbody engine entry into service = min(fps, NGSA) = 2037). My judgement of the likely supplier: P&W about 50%, Rolls-Royce about 30%, CFM about 20%.

4) Commitment by 2035 without pre-emption: 0.65 → 0.55. At 2044 Boeing decides around 2037, so Embraer would have to break its wait-for-Boeing pattern. The Joint Venture also becomes Boeing's best fps form, which raises the chance that Boeing absorbs Embraer.

Strict volume reading: P(100 or more a year exported by 2045 given a launch by 2035) is about 0.2 (judgement, based on the E2 ramp). That gives about 1% (2041) and about 2% (2044).

leading_indicators: Embraer's choice of 'next move': if a large business jet is launched first (2027-30), a commercial launch probably slips past 2035. Watch the investor day and Q4 calls.

A signed funding agreement with money attached (equity, launch aid or risk-sharing amounts) from PIF, the Korean government, Korean Air or KAI, Japan's METI programme, Turkish Aerospace or India. MoUs on structures or E2 production do not count.
An engine MoU or selection for a 25-35k lbf engine with P&W, Rolls-Royce or CFM, and whether the UK funds Rolls-Royce's narrowbody return.
A step-up in Embraer's investment above the current run rate of about $400M a year (2025: $383M), versus a share buyback. A buyback would signal no big programme.
Boeing's narrowbody timing: whether fps or an equivalent is launched around 2034 or slips to about 2037, the 737 rate path (47 → 52 → 63 a month), and any renewed Boeing approach to Embraer.
Airbus capacity beyond 75 a month and the NGSA launch around 2030. Higher Airbus capacity shrinks the vacuum and the entrant's case.
Launch-customer signals for a 180-210 seater from lessors or US and Asian majors, and E195-E2 order strength as a proxy for demand at 150 seats.
COMAC C919 EASA certification (estimated 2028-31) and production reaching 150-200 a year. Either would take part of the same gap and strengthen Airbus's 'now COMAC' deterrent.
New Embraer final-assembly or hub investments abroad (Saudi Arabia, India, Turkey) tied to a new commercial programme.
analysis.impact_on_game:
Fact (board and war game): the delay turns fps from a knife-edge Go into a No-Go. fps 10-year minus Do Nothing goes from +1.06 to -2.53, Boeing is pinned at 20% narrowbody share from 2043, and the war game failed Boeing's go/no-go test. That is what creates the opening for a third player.

Judgement on what this means for the game:

(1) Treat an independent Embraer as a tail risk of about 6% rising to about 11%. It should not drive Boeing's fps decision. Even if Embraer enters, a 100-a-year programme arriving in 2042-45 would mostly fill share the board credits to Airbus but Airbus cannot build ($16.82B PV of NGSA margin above a 1,200-a-year capacity at fps 2044). So a third player is mainly an Airbus risk and a check on Airbus's +$47.6-50.1B delay-world payoff. It does not rescue fps.

(2) Airbus's best response in the delay world is to add capacity, not to use Delay Tactics. Boeing does not launch, so Delay Tactics would only expose Airbus to the $48.32B naked fine. The 400-a-year overflow is the entrant's whole business case.

(3) Re-price 'fps via Embraer' on explicit Joint Venture terms instead of the $100B lump. On the war-game terms it scores +2.21 (2041) and -0.83 (2044). At 2044 that makes it Boeing's best fps form, but it still falls short. A Go needs the partner to carry more than 48% of capex, which Embraer can only do with sovereign co-investors. The board should also add the Joint Venture's denial value: it removes the only plausible non-Chinese entrant.

(4) The engine board cannot value CFM's 'Embraer partnership'. The move exists in code but is never among the 16 CFM moves evaluated. P&W is the engine maker most exposed to, and most likely to back, an independent Embraer.

(5) For the war game, add an Embraer inject. Condition: Boeing has not launched fps by round 3 and Airbus's share is above 70%. Then Embraer launches independently with probability about 0.1, or otherwise offers Boeing a Joint Venture.
caveats: All stage probabilities are my judgement. The ranges multiply the stage ranges, so they are wide on purpose. The point estimates matter less than the ratio: the delay roughly doubles the odds.

check.overall:
FACT BASE: The great majority of factual claims hold. Excel values, transcript quotes, board and war-game parameters and 2024-26 web facts were checked against the files, a re-run of the solve and web searches, and the analyst's solves reproduce exactly (JV +2.21/-0.83, Solo +1.06/-2.53; entrant NPVs; leverage penalty). Errors in the fact base are mostly minor:
- the 2015 investment 'peak' was guidance, not the actual figure;
- single-broker 2030E figures are called consensus;
- the CSeries baseline is wrong;
- the 25% payout is the legal minimum, not a signal;
- the capacity target is stated as one figure where reports give a range.

REASONING: Four inferences are material and need correction.
(1) 'About break-even' for an Embraer entrant comes from the board's convention of paying capex as one lump at entry into service. With realistic spending before EIS, the entrant stays clearly negative (-2.36, or -1.44 with a 5% slice) even after the delay.
(2) 'Boeing decides about 2037, so Embraer must move first' has no source. The war game keeps Boeing's decision in 2031 with a development slip, which would give Embraer the signal it waits for.
(3) 'The delay makes the Joint Venture the preferred form' is not a delay effect on the board. The JV beats Solo at 2041 too, and Solo beats the JV at the war game's $30B capex.
(4) The 2016 'give up a little bit of this market' trigger is about the 104-150 seat segment. It does not support a 180-210 seat clean sheet.
The engine-stage increase is also unsupported, because P&W cancelled GTF2 in both war games.

PROBABILITIES (judgement): The arithmetic and the path totals are internally consistent. The direction (the delay raises the odds) is robust.
